details:
What it does and how it works

CrewVitals is health monitoring software that lets astronauts on long missions check their own health and act on it. On a Mars mission the crew waits about 20 minutes for a message to reach Earth and as long again for the reply, so doctors on the ground cannot help in time. space

A few devices feed the app: a wearable band, a handheld ultrasound scanner, a fluid analyzer, a radiation and cabin sensor unit, and the tablet itself. The readings are grouped into ten body systems, such as heart, bones and muscles, eyes, radiation, sleep and mood. Each reading is compared with that astronaut’s own baseline. A single odd value is only noted, and a sustained drift raises the level. Every body system gets one of four levels: Normal, Watch, Act or Urgent. At Watch or higher, the app explains the change in plain words, gives numbered steps and schedules a re-check.

The main screen shows one sentence on overall status, four key numbers, a body model with a hotspot for each body system, today’s tasks, a chart of vitals over time and a searchable table of every reading.

Benefits

The crew can catch problems early without waiting for Earth. Devices that each measure several things mean less mass to launch and less crew time spent on checks. Plain language and clear steps lower the chance of a wrong response under stress. Each astronaut controls who sees their data.

Intended impact

We want crews on Moon and Mars missions to manage their own health with confidence when Earth is out of reach. The same approach could help people in remote places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and rural clinics, where a doctor is also far away.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The front end is designed in TypeScript with React and Vite. It uses Tailwind CSS for styling, shadcn/ui for components, Recharts for charts, TanStack Table for the records table and Lucide for icons. It runs on realistic mock data at this stage. The devices are a concept and have not been built.

How it is creative

  • The body model is the menu. The astronaut taps the part of the body they are worried about and does not have to search through lists.
  • The look mixes a dark space console, a health dashboard and a retro green terminal with its own mascot, so a medical tool feels like part of the ship.
  • Two voices share the screen. Short system lines report state, and a friendly voice explains anything about health.
  • Trend colors follow meaning, not direction. A rising heart rate shows red, and rising sleep shows green.

Factors we considered

  • Delay and loss of contact: everything needed to assess and act is stored on board, and the app works fully offline.
  • The full range of risks: the ten body systems cover the five spaceflight hazards named by NASA’s Human Research Program, which are space radiation, altered gravity, isolation and confinement, closed environments and distance from Earth. nih
  • Individual differences: each person is judged against their own baseline, because a value that is normal for one astronaut can be a warning for another.
  • Crew time and attention: the daily check takes under two minutes, and each alert comes with one clear next step.
  • Privacy: health data stays private unless the astronaut shares it. Urgent alerts are the exception and always reach the crew medical officer.
  • The cabin: a dark theme for dim light, large touch targets for a floating user, and status shown by color, icon and word together.
  • Stress: the tone stays calm, and only an Urgent alert may flash.

Only the text above the line is for the form. It is about 600 words.
